We start by defining our unknowns.

  • Let the number of hours per week Ouma will work at Job I be \( x \).
  • Let the number of hours per week Ouma will work at Job II be \( y \).

Now we write the objective function. Since Ouma gets paid \(\text{KSh }{@cc@}\) an hour at Job I, and \(\text{KSh }{@dd@}\) an hour at Job II, his total income \( I \) is given by the following equation:

\( \qquad \qquad I = {@cc@}x + {@dd@}y \)

The next task is to find the constraints. The second sentence in the problem states, "He never wants to work more than a total of \({@aa@}\) hours a week." This translates into the following constraint:

\( \qquad \qquad {@x1*x@} + {@x2*y@} \leq {@aa@} \)

The third sentence states, "For every hour he works at Job I, he needs \({@y1@}\) hours of preparation time, and for every hour he works at Job II, he needs \({@y2@}\) hour(s) of preparation time, and he cannot spend more than \({@bb@}\) hours for preparation." The translation follows.

\( \qquad \qquad {@y1*x@} + {@y2*y@} \leq {@bb@} \)

Then we have the non-negativity constraints: \( x \geq 0 \) and \( y\geq 0 \).

Now we have the Formulated Problem:

\( \qquad \text{Maximize} \quad I = {@cc@}x + {@dd@}y \)

\( \qquad \qquad \text{Subject to:} \quad \begin{cases} {@x1*x@} + {@x2*y@} \leq {@aa@} \\ {@y1*x@} + {@y2*y@} \leq {@bb@} \\ x \geq 0, \quad y \geq 0 \end{cases} \)

Graphing the Constraints and Finding the Feasible Region

In order to solve the problem, we graph the constraints and shade the region that satisfies all the inequality constraints.

Any appropriate method can be used to graph the lines for the constraints. However, often the easiest method is to graph the line by plotting the \(x\)-intercept and \(y\)-intercept.

The line for a constraint will divide the plane into two regions, one of which satisfies the inequality part of the constraint. A test point is used to determine which portion of the plane to shade to satisfy the inequality. Any point on the plane that is not on the line can be used as a test point.

  • If the test point satisfies the inequality, then the region of the plane that satisfies the inequality is the region that contains the test point.
  • If the test point does not satisfy the inequality, then the region that satisfies the inequality lies on the opposite side of the line from the test point.

After the lines representing the constraints were graphed, the point \( (0,0) \) was used as a test point to determine that:

  • The point \( (0,0) \) satisfies the constraint \( {@x1*x@} + {@x2*y@} \leq {@aa@} \) because: \( 0+0 < {@aa@} \).
  • The point \( (0,0) \) satisfies the constraint \( {@y1*x@} + {@y2*y@} \leq {@bb@} \) because: \( {@y1@}(0) + {@y2@}(0)<{@bb@} \).

Note that the constraints \( x \geq 0 \) and \(y \geq 0 \) have also been applied.

\(b.)\) The demand for product \(II\) is not more than \(\frac{1}{{@a5@}}\) the demand for product \(I\).

\(c.)\) The production level of product \(I\) is less than or equal to \({@a4@}\) kg plus \({@a6@}\) times the production level of product \(II\).

Worked solution

Given the minimization problem:

\(\begin{align} \text{Minimize } Z &= {@ c1 * x_1@} + {@c2 * x_2@} \end{align}\)

Subject to:

\(\begin{align} {@constraint1@} \\ {@constraint2@} \\ x_1 &\geq 0; \quad x_2 \geq 0 \\ \end{align}\)

To achieve our goal, we first express our problem as the following matrix.

\[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} {@ a11@} & {@ a12@} & & {@b1@} \\ {@ a21@} & {@ a22@} & & {@b2@}\\ \hline {@c1@} & {@c2@} & & 0 \end{array} \]

Observe that this table looks like an initial simplex tableau without the slack variables. Next, we write a matrix whose columns are the rows of this matrix, and the rows are the columns. Such a matrix is called a transpose of the original matrix. We get:

\[ \begin{array}{ccc|c} {@ a11@} & {@ a21@} & & {@c1@} \\ {@ a12@} & {@ a22@} & & {@c2@}\\ \hline {@b1@} & {@b2@} & & 0 \end{array} \]

The following maximization problem associated with the above matrix is called its dual.

\(\begin{align} \text{Maximize } Z &= {@ b1 * y_1@} + {@b2 * y_2@} \end{align}\)

Subject to:

\(\begin{align} {@dual_constraint1@} \\ {@dual_constraint2@} \\ y_1 &\geq 0; \quad y_2 \geq 0 \\ \end{align}\)

In order to solve its dual using the simplex method, we first introduce slack variables \( s_1 \) and \( s_2 \) for the inequalities:

\[ \begin{align} {@dual_constraint1_1@} \\ {@dual_constraint2_1@} \\ y_1 &\geq 0; \quad y_2 \geq 0 \\ \end{align} \]

The initial simplex tableau is:

\[ \begin{array}{c|ccccc|c} & y_1 & y_2 & s_1 & s_2 & Z & C \\ \hline & {@a11@} & {@a21@} & 1 & 0 & 0 & {@c1@} \\ & {@a12@}&{@a22@} & 0 & 1 & 0 & {@c2@} \\ \hline & -{@b1@}& -{@b2@} & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ \end{array} \]

Observe an important change. Here our main variables are \(y_1 \) and \(y_2\) and the slack variables are \(s_1 \) and \(s_2\).

In order to find the final simplex tableau proceed using the simplex algorithm.

Correct application of the Simplex Algorithm should yield the the optimal solution of the dual problem to be \({@w_opt@}\) and this occurs when \(y_{1}={@yy1@}\) and \(y_{2}={@yy2@}\). Now the Slack variables in this solution are \(s_{1}={@xx1@}\) and \(s_{2}={@xx2@}\).

generalfeedback.text:
✍ Worked Solution

We start by defining our unknowns.

  • Let the number of hours per week Ouma will work at Job I be \( x \).
  • Let the number of hours per week Ouma will work at Job II be \( y \).

Now we write the objective function. Since Ouma gets paid \(\text{KSh }{@cc@}\) an hour at Job I, and \(\text{KSh }{@dd@}\) an hour at Job II, his total income \( I \) is given by the following equation:

\( \qquad \qquad I = {@cc@}x + {@dd@}y \)

The next task is to find the constraints. The second sentence in the problem states, "He never wants to work more than a total of \({@aa@}\) hours a week." This translates into the following constraint:

\( \qquad \qquad {@x1*x@} + {@x2*y@} \leq {@aa@} \)

The third sentence states, "For every hour he works at Job I, he needs \({@y1@}\) hours of preparation time, and for every hour he works at Job II, he needs \({@y2@}\) hour(s) of preparation time, and he cannot spend more than \({@bb@}\) hours for preparation." The translation follows.

\( \qquad \qquad {@y1*x@} + {@y2*y@} \leq {@bb@} \)

Then we have the non-negativity constraints: \( x \geq 0 \) and \( y\geq 0 \).

Now we have the Formulated Problem:

\( \qquad \text{Maximize} \quad I = {@cc@}x + {@dd@}y \)

\( \qquad \qquad \text{Subject to:} \quad \begin{cases} {@x1*x@} + {@x2*y@} \leq {@aa@} \\ {@y1*x@} + {@y2*y@} \leq {@bb@} \\ x \geq 0, \quad y \geq 0 \end{cases} \)

Graphing the Constraints and Finding the Feasible Region

In order to solve the problem, we graph the constraints and shade the region that satisfies all the inequality constraints.

Any appropriate method can be used to graph the lines for the constraints. However, often the easiest method is to graph the line by plotting the \(x\)-intercept and \(y\)-intercept.

The line for a constraint will divide the plane into two regions, one of which satisfies the inequality part of the constraint. A test point is used to determine which portion of the plane to shade to satisfy the inequality. Any point on the plane that is not on the line can be used as a test point.

  • If the test point satisfies the inequality, then the region of the plane that satisfies the inequality is the region that contains the test point.
  • If the test point does not satisfy the inequality, then the region that satisfies the inequality lies on the opposite side of the line from the test point.

After the lines representing the constraints were graphed, the point \( (0,0) \) was used as a test point to determine that:

  • The point \( (0,0) \) satisfies the constraint \( {@x1*x@} + {@x2*y@} \leq {@aa@} \) because: \( 0+0 < {@aa@} \).
  • The point \( (0,0) \) satisfies the constraint \( {@y1*x@} + {@y2*y@} \leq {@bb@} \) because: \( {@y1@}(0) + {@y2@}(0)<{@bb@} \).

Note that the constraints \( x \geq 0 \) and \(y \geq 0 \) have also been applied.
